content: The number of individuals with chronic hepatitis B is determined by identifying those with a positive HBsAg serological status. The total population serves as the denominator for calculating prevalence. These estimates may be derived from older or contemporary biomarker surveys conducted in specific populations of interest. Modeling can also incorporate routine surveillance data, such as testing data, while accounting for methodological limitations and population representativeness. Relevant input parameters for modeling include the number of individuals treated over time, vaccination coverage, HBV infection incidence, and liver-related or general population deaths. Data mining and triangulation from routine surveillance testing, such as among blood donors and pregnant women, are also utilized. Disaggregation of data is recommended by sex/gender, age groups, geographical location, pregnancy status, and populations at high risk of infection or with a high burden of hepatitis B. If possible, data should distinguish between current infection (HBsAg) and evidence of past or present infection (anti-HBc), as well as HIV and HDV coinfection status. Ageand sex-disaggregated prevalence should then be applied to calculate the total infected population. Global reporting platforms include the WHO Global Hepatitis Reporting System and consolidated guidelines on person-centered viral hepatitis strategic information. These guidelines aim to support countries in scaling up hepatitis prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services. This indicator reflects the epidemic's scale and service needs, serving as a numerator or denominator for other indicators along the result chain. The presence of anti-HCV antibodies indicates past or present infection but does not distinguish between resolved or active infection. Recommended biomarkers for chronic hepatitis C include HCV RNA and HCV core antigen. Understanding the prevalence of chronic hepatitis C helps programs assess the burden of disease and plan testing, care, and treatment services accordingly. The availability and readiness of HBV and HCV drugs and diagnostics are assessed by measuring service readiness, which includes the presence of trained staff, guidelines, equipment, diagnostics, and medicines. Service availability refers to the physical presence of services, such as infrastructure and staff, as well as the availability of specific services in facilities. Indicators include the percentage of facilities offering hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination, onsite testing for hepatitis B and C using molecular, serological, or rapid test methods, and antiviral therapy for hepatitis B and C. This indicator reflects access to vaccination at birth and progress toward eliminating vertical transmission of HBV. Disaggregation includes age, place of birth, residence, sex, and socioeconomic status. This indicator monitors immunization program performance and progress toward eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HBV. Testing coverage among pregnant women for HBsAg is critical for their health and preventing mother-to-child transmission of HBV. This indicator informs programs about necessary interventions to strengthen elimination efforts and monitor exposed infants. It also provides information on the prevalence of chronic hepatitis B among pregnant women and guides epidemic dynamics. This indicator reflects sustained service quality during antenatal care and monitors progress toward eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HBV. The proportion of exposed newborns receiving HBV immunoglobulin according to national policy is another critical indicator for validating the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HBV. Data sources include program records, maternity registers, and sentinel surveillance. This indicator tracks the progress of needle and syringe programs in providing sterile injecting equipment to reduce the risk of hepatitis and other infections. This intervention reduces injecting frequency and supports the treatment of other health conditions, such as HIV, tuberculosis, and viral hepatitis. Data sources include program records and population size estimates of opioid-dependent individuals who inject drugs.
